title: Sleep, stress, pollution and sensitive skin: a 151-woman cross-sectional study across two cities
headline: Sensitive skin carried more oxidative damage in both cities, and an inflammation marker was nearly three times higher in the busier city; but sleep, stress, pollution and city moved together, so none of them can be blamed on its own.
evidenceTier: Cross-sectional, 151 women, industry-affiliated authors, unadjusted; full text read
fit: A reminder of what an exposome study can and cannot tell you. It supports the idea that lifestyle context shapes skin, but gives no intervention to try and no deep-skin data.
displaces: Fits nowhere as a product; it informs how much weight to give single-factor stress and sleep claims.
estimateNote: Prices marked EST are my guesses, not looked up.
summaryPoints: Cross-sectional (full text read): 151 Chinese women aged 35 to 50 in a high-pollution big city and a lower-pollution coastal city; sensitive skin in the big city had 17.9% more protein carbonylation than non-sensitive skin in the same city.

Within sensitive skin, prostaglandin E2 was 185% higher in the big city (4.36 vs 1.53 pg/ug protein), with more sebum and visible pores; the coastal city had more pigment spots and oxidative damage (UV not measured).
Everyone in the big-city group slept under 7 hours with higher stress scores and everyone in the other group the reverse, so sleep, stress, pollution and UV are inseparable here.
Several authors work for a skincare company; analyses were exploratory and unadjusted.
fitLine: Context for lifestyle claims, not an intervention; no deep-skin data.

fitAxes.why: Water loss was not higher in sensitive skin in this cohort.
Sebum and pores were higher in the heavily urban group; breakouts were not assessed.
UV-exposed coastal setting went with more pigment and oxidative damage, but sun use was not measured.

dossier.whatItIs: A cross-sectional comparison of 151 Chinese women aged 35 to 50 (Fitzpatrick II to IV) in two cities, grouped by self-reported skin sensitivity and by lifestyle (pollution, sleep and perceived stress). Skin surface samples were assayed for an inflammation marker (prostaglandin E2) and an oxidative-damage marker (protein carbonylation), alongside imaging and instruments.

steps: Sensitive skin (a self-reported score) was associated with higher protein carbonylation and more dark spots than non-sensitive skin in the same city.
Within sensitive skin, the city with higher pollution, shorter sleep and higher perceived stress had much higher prostaglandin E2, more sebum and more visible pores.
The city with lower pollution and better sleep but higher UV (a coastal city) had more pigment spots and more oxidative damage.
Because sleep, stress, pollution, UV and climate all differ by city, the study cannot say which exposure drives which marker.
mechanism.inferenceFlag: Sleep and stress group membership was perfectly aligned with city (100% of the high-urban group slept under 7 hours with stress scores of 18 or more; 100% of the other group slept over 7 hours with scores of 14 or less). They cannot be separated from pollution, UV or climate. Any link from stress or sleep to prostaglandin E2 here is an association, not a mechanism.
mechanism.diagramCaption: Urban exposome (pollution + short sleep + high stress; not separable) -> higher prostaglandin E2, sebum, pores (observed) | High-UV coastal setting -> more pigment spots, oxidative damage (observed)

studies.cite: Conway J, Berlin I, Blanche C, Grivet-Seyve M, Wai HD, Tonetti NJ, et al. Lifestyle-driven phenotypes in sensitive skin: a cross-sectional, multicenter study across urbanization tiers. Dermatol Ther (Heidelb). 2026;16(11):5701-5712.
studies.design: Cross-sectional, two sites (Guangzhou and Xiamen, China), March to April 2024, run by a contract research organisation. 151 women, 35 to 50 years, Fitzpatrick II to IV. Groups: non-sensitive skin, high-urban lifestyle (n=50); sensitive skin, high-urban (n=50); sensitive skin, moderate-urban (n=51). Sensitivity by the Sensitive Scale-10 (no objective provocation test). Perceived Stress Scale-10 and a sleep scale defined lifestyle. VISIA-CR imaging, Tewameter, Sebumeter, tape-strip assays for protein carbonylation and prostaglandin E2.
studies.who: Healthy women resident at least 5 years in the same city with stable lifestyle; no sleep, stress or antidepressant medication. Phototype distribution differed between groups (more phototype II in the coastal group). Deeper skin tones (V to VI) were not included.
results: Prostaglandin E2 (pg/ug protein): 3.53 non-sensitive high-urban, 4.36 sensitive high-urban, 1.53 sensitive moderate-urban.
Protein carbonylation: 0.28, 0.33, 0.42 respectively. Dark spot clinical score: 2.45, 3.38, 4.32.
Water loss through the skin (TEWL) was comparable across groups, so sensitivity was not associated with a measured barrier deficit.
studies.effectSize: Percentages as stated in results (above). Unadjusted group comparisons.
studies.material: Not established. These are biomarker and imaging associations, not symptoms or treatment effects.
studies.conflict: Several authors are Galderma R&D employees (a skincare company); the study was run by a contract research organisation.
studies.limits: Cross-sectional; two cities differ in pollution, UV, climate and probably income and diet; sleep and stress perfectly aligned with city; not adjusted for age, phototype or multiple comparisons (authors call it exploratory); sun protection and individual UV exposure not measured; self-reported sensitivity; Chinese women only.

claimsCheck.claim: Poor sleep and high stress raise skin inflammation (prostaglandin E2)
claimsCheck.status: Not shown: sleep, stress, pollution and city all differ together, so the study cannot isolate any one

claimsCheck.claim: Sensitive skin is a distinct biological state
claimsCheck.status: Partly: protein carbonylation was higher in sensitive skin in both cities; sensitivity was not defined by an objective test

howToUse: Nothing to adopt. If anything, this is a reminder that exposome questions (sleep, stress, air quality, UV) come as a bundle, so a single intervention is hard to credit or blame.

The authors suggest tailoring care to the dominant exposure (anti-inflammatory in heavily urban settings, antioxidant and photoprotective in high-UV settings) but that is a hypothesis they did not test.
wouldChangeVerdict: A trial that improves sleep or lowers stress (for example breathing training or a sleep programme) and measures prostaglandin E2 and pigment in the same people
A cohort that measures sleep, stress, pollution and UV separately in the same city
Replication in deeper skin tones and outside China
dossier.transfer: Does it transfer to deeper skin? Participants were Fitzpatrick II to IV, so tone V to VI is untested. The question of whether stress and sleep affect skin inflammation and pigment is physiological, not tone-specific, but this study cannot confirm it (inference).
confidence: Not verified: biomarker assay validation, funding statement wording, sleep and stress scores per participant.
Industry-affiliated authors; exploratory analyses without multiplicity correction.
